identification.summary: Russian military intelligence (GRU) cyber unit responsible for most of the destructive and disruptive cyberattacks against Ukraine over the past decade, including the 2015 and 2016 power-grid outages, NotPetya (2017), and wipers deployed around the February 2022 invasion [S2][S3]. It combines espionage, sabotage and information operations, and paces its attacks to support Russian conventional military operations [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly documented destructive activity since at least the December 2015 Ukraine grid outage; the 2020 DOJ indictment covers attacks from 2015 to 2019 [S2][S3]. Earlier espionage activity under the Sandworm name is reported in the imported references but was not re-verified here. Microsoft's BadPilot subgroup has been active since at least 2021 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Seashell Blizzard (formerly IRIDIUM). Microsoft maps Sandworm, VOODOO BEAR, APT44, UAC-0113, BE2 and BlackEnergy Lite to it [S8]. Mandiant upgraded the cluster to APT44 in April 2024 to separate it from APT28 (GRU Unit 26165) [S3].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation: GRU Unit 74455, the Main Centre for Special Technologies (GTsST) of the Main Directorate of the General Staff [S1][S2][S3].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution through the October 2020 indictment of six named Unit 74455 officers [S2]. Microsoft states the actor works on behalf of GRU Unit 74455 [S1]. ESET attributes the December 2025 Poland wiper attempt with medium confidence [S6].
attribution.basis: DOJ indictment evidence [S2]; long-running vendor forensics (Mandiant, ESET, Microsoft, Dragos) [S1][S3][S4][S6]; malware lineage across BlackEnergy, Industroyer/Industroyer2, NotPetya and later wipers.

objectives: Support Russian military and political objectives through destructive and disruptive attacks, intelligence collection and influence operations, focused on Ukraine and increasingly on states supporting it [S1][S3]. Targets Western elections and institutions, including in NATO countries [S3]. Microsoft assesses its access subgroup exists to establish and hold access in sectors of interest to Russia, which can later enable destructive operations [S1].

regions: NATO and EU states, including Poland (Dec 2025 energy-sector wiper attempt)
United States, Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom (BadPilot focus in 2024)
Central Asia and the Middle East (BadPilot, 2023)
targeting.notes: Sector and region data from Mandiant [S3], Microsoft's BadPilot reporting [S1] and ESET [S6]. Ukrainian water and heating targeting as reported in ESET-derived coverage [S6].

capabilities.summary: Full-spectrum: espionage, destructive wipers and OT effects. OT capability is proven: Industroyer (2016), Industroyer2 against a Ukrainian substation (thwarted April 2022) [S5], and an October 2022 outage caused by executing native MicroSCADA binaries (scilc.exe), a living-off-the-land approach to OT [S4]. Wipers include NotPetya, KillDisk, CaddyWiper and DynoWiper (Poland, Dec 2025) [S2][S4][S6]. Initial access through edge devices and n-day exploits (Exchange CVE-2021-34473, Zimbra CVE-2022-41352, ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709, FortiClient EMS CVE-2023-48788), with persistence through RMM tools (Atera, Splashtop), the ShadowLink Tor hidden-service tool and the LocalOlive web shell [S1]. Uses hacktivist-branded Telegram personas for influence [S3].

campaigns.name: Ukraine power outage (BlackEnergy)
campaigns.summary: First publicly confirmed grid outage caused by a cyberattack; attributed to Sandworm by Mandiant and named in the 2020 DOJ indictment.

campaigns.name: Industroyer / CrashOverride
campaigns.summary: Second Ukraine grid attack using malware purpose-built to speak ICS protocols to substation equipment.

campaigns.name: NotPetya
campaigns.summary: Destructive malware launched against Ukraine spread worldwide through multinational networks; nearly $1 billion in losses to three victims named in the indictment alone.

campaigns.name: Olympic Destroyer
campaigns.summary: Attack on the PyeongChang Winter Olympics with false flags pointing at North Korea.

campaigns.name: DOJ indictment
campaigns.summary: Six GRU Unit 74455 officers charged for NotPetya, the Ukraine grid attacks, Olympic Destroyer and other operations.

campaigns.name: Industroyer2 (thwarted)
campaigns.summary: CERT-UA, with ESET and Microsoft, prevented a planned attack on a Ukrainian energy provider's substations.

campaigns.name: OT-induced outage via MicroSCADA
campaigns.summary: Mandiant documents a power outage caused by native MicroSCADA commands, followed two days later by CaddyWiper in IT. Reported 2023-11-09.

campaigns.name: BadPilot access subgroup
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports a Seashell Blizzard subgroup running global opportunistic access operations, expanding from Ukraine (2022) to the US, UK, Canada and Australia (2024). It likely enabled at least three destructive attacks in Ukraine since 2023.

campaigns.name: Poland energy-sector wiper attempt
campaigns.summary: DynoWiper deployed against Polish energy organizations, including combined heat and power plants and a renewables management system. Execution was blocked; ESET attributes it to Sandworm with medium confidence.

diamond.adversary: GRU Unit 74455 (GTsST); six officers named in the 2020 DOJ indictment [S2].
diamond.capability: OT-specific malware (Industroyer, Industroyer2) and OT living-off-the-land; wipers (NotPetya, KillDisk, CaddyWiper, DynoWiper); n-day edge exploitation; RMM-based persistence; ShadowLink; hacktivist personas [S1][S3][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised edge devices and internet-facing servers; RMM services for C2; Tor hidden services via ShadowLink; Telegram personas for influence and leak operations [S1][S3].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian energy, government, telecom, water and heating; NATO-state energy (Poland); global energy, oil and gas, shipping, telecoms and arms manufacturing reached through BadPilot [S1][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Coercion and sabotage aligned with Russian war aims in Ukraine and pressure on states supporting Ukraine; election interference [S3].
diamond.technology: IT-to-OT pivot through Windows domain and SCADA management hosts; reuse of native vendor tools to avoid OT-specific malware signatures [S4].

gaps: Relationship between the BadPilot access subgroup and Sandworm's destructive teams: how accesses are handed off and prioritized is not public [S1].
Extent of BadPilot access in US, UK, Canadian and Australian networks after Microsoft's 2025 disclosure.

Primary-source confirmation still needed: the DOJ 2020 indictment, the Mandiant APT44 report and ESET's Industroyer2 analysis were verified through coverage only, because those sites were blocked from this environment.
Operational coordination between Seashell Blizzard and other GRU units (Forest Blizzard / APT28, Cadet Blizzard) in shared campaigns.
Whether the Poland attempt reflects an intent change toward NATO critical infrastructure or opportunistic access use.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: For any EUCOM or NATO contingency, the cyberspace OE includes allied energy, heating, water and telecom OT, not just DoD networks. Poland in Dec 2025 shows NATO-state energy is in range. STEP 2: Sandworm times effects with kinetic operations, so cyber effects should be modeled alongside the adversary's fires and maneuver timeline, not as a separate line. STEP 3: The template is edge or n-day initial access (often prepared long in advance by BadPilot), then domain compromise, then pivot to SCADA management hosts, then OT effect using native tools, then wiper to destroy evidence and slow recovery. STEP 4: MLCOA is sustained espionage and access maintenance in allied energy and logistics with periodic destructive attacks in Ukraine. MDCOA is synchronized wiper and OT attacks on allied energy and logistics nodes supporting reinforcement of NATO's eastern flank. Candidate indicators: RMM tools (Atera, Splashtop) appearing without change records, Tor hidden-service persistence, new local admin accounts on SCADA management hosts, and abnormal MicroSCADA or engineering tool execution [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Integrate allied CERT reporting (CERT-UA, Polish CSIRTs) and vendor ICS telemetry into shared situational awareness, since the earliest warning is often in partner OT networks. (2) Plan for degraded host-nation infrastructure: C2 resilience and mission assurance assessments should assume possible power and heating loss at staging areas. (3) Authorities: defense of allied civilian infrastructure is a host-nation lead. US cyber forces support through partner agreements and hunt-forward-type missions, which must be coordinated through EUCOM and USCYBERCOM channels. (4) Wiper resilience: offline backups and restoration drills for deployed mission systems are a C2 continuity requirement, not just an IT task.
